newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Dec broad money leaves rate rise issue hazy.
newsitem.headline: Polish Dec broad money leaves rate rise issue hazy.

text.p: The release of Polish December broad money data on Tuesday did little to ease the uncertainty surrounding a possible official interest rate rise by the National Bank of Poland, analysts said.
Last month broad money jumped 5.1 percent or 6.6 billion zlotys, against 1.4 percent in November and 2.1 in December 1995, the NBP said. @

"The money supply figures did not clarify the interest rate picture and now we will wait until Wednesday for the release of December inflation data," Marcin Stefaniuk, senior dealer at BDK SA bank told Reuters.
The Central Statistical Office (GUS) is sheduled to release December figures after 1200 GMT on Wednesday.
Analysts expected CPI to fall to 18.8 percent in December from 19.1 in November and 21.6 at the end of 1995, while the finance ministry said it would be at 18.4-18.6 percent. @
The central bank said nearly half of the broad money jump could be attributed to end-of-the-year seasonal factors and changes in account regulations.

Deputy NBP president Witold Kozinski said the clearing of float money, cash tied up in clearing operations, may have added between 2.5 to three billion zlotys and interest payments another one billion zlotys to last month's broad money data.

"Banks cleared much of the so-called float money before a change of account numbers as of January 1," Kozinski told Reuters in a brief telephone interview, adding that total float money amounted to some 4.7 billion zlotys in November 1996. @
Kozinski said broad money supply should stay relatively flat in January or could even fall in nominal terms this month.

Many market players expected the central bank to cosmetically raise official interest rates, now at 25 and 22 percent, after increasing market rates to by some 2.5 points over the last few weeks to stop quick growing credit action.
In 1996 credit to the non-financial sector increased by 43 percent, of which credit to households a whopping 109 percent.
However, Poland's credit rise was accompanied by an even larger rise in deposits, counted in nominal terms, which analysts said was a good singal for the developing economy. @

"Credit boomed in 1996, but it was accompanied by a steady growth of deposits, rising some 44 percent for households, which is a healthy sign," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at the Centre of Strategic Studies, the former planning ministry.
